notes.1ai: This was answered very well, with most candidates gaining full credit. A common error was to add all three forces.
notes.1aii: Not all candidates recognised that the lorry would continue at the same speed if there was no resultant force acting.
notes.1bi: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer.
notes.1bii: Often more detailed answers were needed. For example, answers simply stating “friction” or “speed” were too vague. The question asked for a factor that could increase the total stopping distance, so “reduced friction” or “higher speed” would have been sufficient.
notes.2ai: Most candidates attempted this part with many getting the correct answer and unit. A common error was to multiply the weight by 10 instead of dividing by 10.
notes.2aii: Many candidates answered this question well and showed full working. Weaker candidates often gained partial credit for the moments equation, gave an incorrect answer with no working or gave no response. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics November 2020
notes.2b: Many correct answers were seen for the force. A common incorrect answer was kinetic energy.
notes.3ai: The majority of candidates gave the full answer of gravitational potential (energy).
notes.3aii: Few correct answers were seen, and many candidates did not seem to fully understand that work done = energy transferred.
notes.3b: Again, candidates did not seem to fully understand that work done = energy transferred. Many recognised that work was being done when moving a chair but fewer understood that energy was being transferred when stretching a spring.
notes.3c: The vast majority of candidates gave the correct answers.
notes.4a: Most candidates gained credit for stating that the vehicle did not sink into the mud. For further credit candidates needed to give a more detailed answer based on the idea that pressure = force/area. A number of candidates did not give an answer for this question.
notes.4bi: Candidates generally lacked the knowledge for this part, and air was a common incorrect answer.
notes.4bii: There was some confusion between a barometer and a thermometer, and the most common incorrect answer was temperature .
notes.4ci: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer.
notes.4cii: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer.
notes.5a: The vast majority of candidates gave the correct answer.
notes.5bi: Many candidates gave the correct answer. A significant number thought that an increase in temperature would cause the air molecules to move more slowly.
notes.5bii: Most candidates gave the correct answer. However. some candidates either incorrectly repeated or rephrased their answer to the previous part of this question.
notes.5ci: Few candidates fully understood the terminology associated with a liquid-in-glass thermometer.
notes.5cii: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer.
notes.5ciii: Many candidates were able to describe that the liquid would move up the tube. Very few were able to explain that this was due to the liquid expanding.
notes.6a: A more thorough description of the thermal processes involved, particularly convection, was required. Most answers were vague or focused on molecules moving faster.
notes.6bi: There appeared to be confusion regarding the effect of colour and texture of a surface on the emission of radiation. Very few correct answers were seen.
notes.6bii: Many candidates were able to suggest a change that would reduce the loss of thermal energy. Very few were able to then explain how their suggestion achieved the reduction. The most common correct suggestion and explanation were to wrap the can in cotton wool to reduce heat lost by conduction. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics November 2020
notes.7a: Many candidates gained some credit here. The most common error was thinking blue (or violet) was the colour that was refracted least.
notes.7bi: (ii) Many correct answers were seen here. A common error was selecting the angles between the mirror and the rays rather than the angles between the rays and the normal.
notes.8a: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer. There was some confusion between the symbol for a fuse and a thermistor.
notes.8bi: Many candidates answered this question well. Weaker candidates often used an incorrect equation i.e. potential difference = current divided by resistance or gave no response.
notes.8bii: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer. A common incorrect answer was ammeter. A few candidates did not give an answer for this question.
notes.8biii: Many candidates knew the symbol for a voltmeter but placing it in parallel with the resistor proved to be more challenging. Several candidates did not give an answer for this question.
notes.9a: Many candidates knew that magnetism was involved. A fuller explanation was required to gain further credit.
notes.9bi: Few correct answers were seen with many candidates offering brief statements or no response. The magnetic properties of iron and electromagnets did not seem to be fully understood.
notes.9bii: Very few candidates recognised that the bell had its own battery.
notes.10a: Candidates generally lacked the knowledge needed for this question. There were a considerable number of blank responses. Answers often only gained credit for drawing a wire between the poles of a magnet.
notes.10b: Many candidates correctly recognised that the current needed to be reduced in some way. A number of candidates did not give an answer for this question.
notes.11a: Most candidates identified the isotopes, and many gave the correct explanation. However, there was some confusion between the terms proton, neutron and nucleon.
notes.11bi: Many correct answers were seen. Other answers were too vague or repeated part of the question i.e. “damages people”.
notes.11bii: Candidates were usually able to state how radiographers could be protected. Fewer were able to give an explanation. A common, correct answer was to suggest wearing a lead apron as the apron absorbs X-rays. There was a noticeable number of blank responses.
notes.11ci: A few correct answers were seen. There was some confusion between the penetrating abilities of radioactive emissions. Several candidates did not give an answer for this question.
notes.11cii: Only the strongest candidates answered this question correctly. Several incorrect answers accounted for the reading on the meter by naming a region of the electromagnetic spectrum. A number of candidates did not give an answer. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics November 2020
